Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "When Mara Ellis began the family photo catalogue, she expected to sort boxes by decade and write down the names she could still remember. Instead, the project quickly became a record of how relatives wanted their pictures handled. Her aunt June had kept photographs in biscuit tins beneath a guest-room bed, while Mara's father stored loose prints in labeled envelopes. The two collections overlapped, but each carried different notes, dates, and assumptions about who should be allowed to see them. Mara set up a shared catalogue so everyone could identify people and correct details, then discovered that a single family archive did not mean every image belonged in every relative's inbox.

The first working session took place at June's kitchen table. Mara brought a laptop, cotton gloves, and a small scanner; June made tea and arranged the prints into rough piles. They started with a 1968 picnic at Lake Windermere, where a handwritten caption named six people but omitted a child standing near the edge of the frame. June recognized him as her cousin Peter, who had died before Mara was born. She asked Mara to record the name, but not to send the picture to Peter's former partner, Helen. “She has her own copy of the group shot,” June said. “This one shows the back of the house, and I don't know whether she'd want it.” Mara entered the identification and left the sharing field unset until they could ask Peter's daughter.

That pause led Mara to separate description from distribution. Each catalogue record received a title, approximate date, location, people shown, source box, and a note about the physical print. A different field listed who could view a digital copy. At first she used a single family-wide group, because it seemed simple and familiar. Her cousin Sam pointed out that the group included teenagers, former spouses, and relatives who had not spoken in years. He also reminded her that a public-facing family tree could expose an image even when no one had sent it directly. Mara revised the plan so that a name in a caption did not automatically grant access to the photograph.

She wrote a short set of working rules and taped them beside the scanner. The rules were not a legal statement or a claim that everyone had agreed to every detail. They were a way to keep decisions visible while the catalogue grew. Mara asked relatives to flag errors without replacing somebody else's description silently, and she kept a dated note whenever a permission changed. If a photograph showed a person who had asked not to be included in family sharing, Mara would leave that person out of the searchable name list and restrict the image while she checked the request. She did not assume that a relative's permission covered a spouse, child, or guest in the same frame.

1. Record what is visible before guessing why the photograph was taken.
2. Mark uncertain dates as estimates, and keep the source of each estimate.
3. Ask the person shown, when possible, before widening access to a sensitive image.
4. Keep an original scan unchanged; make a separate copy for cropping or repairs.
5. Note who requested a restriction and when it should be reviewed.

The numbered list helped during a later visit from Mara's brother, Lewis, who brought a folder from their grandmother's flat. One print showed a birthday meal in 1984, with their grandmother seated beside a woman neither sibling recognized. Lewis thought she might be a neighbor; Mara wondered whether she was a nurse who had helped after their grandmother's surgery. Rather than choose one description, they entered “unidentified guest” and added both suggestions to the research note. The back of the print carried the words “Sunday, after the hospital,” but no month or year. Mara photographed the inscription and linked it to the record, keeping the date field at “approximately 1984” instead of turning a clue into a certainty.

Their family members did not respond to the new catalogue in one uniform way. Cousin Priya enjoyed correcting place names and sent a scanned map of the old neighborhood. Uncle David preferred paper copies and asked Mara to mail him a small index, not create an online account for him. Two younger relatives offered to identify classmates in a school photograph, but one asked that their own names not appear in search results. Mara recorded those preferences separately. She also kept a list of outstanding questions, including whether a reunion photograph could be shared with the wider group and whether a picture of June's former apartment contained a visible address. The list showed what still needed attention without suggesting that a decision had already been made.

A practical problem arose when Mara prepared a batch of scans for review. The catalogue platform generated preview images automatically, and those previews were visible to everyone in the test group. She noticed that one restricted portrait appeared in a thumbnail even though its full-size file was unavailable. Mara removed that batch from the shared folder, checked the remaining previews, and changed the access settings before inviting relatives back. She wrote down which files had been exposed to the test group and contacted the three people who had been reviewing them. No one asked her to delete the underlying family records, but the incident made the distinction between a record and a shareable copy important to everyone involved.

By autumn, the catalogue held images from four households, with many dates still approximate and several names unresolved. Mara kept the original envelopes and boxes in their owners' homes rather than treating the project as a reason to collect them. A small backup drive stayed with her father, and a second copy was stored in a labeled case at June's house. The family planned another sorting afternoon for winter, when Lewis could bring the album he had found in a storage cupboard. Until then, Mara's last entry was a note about a faded ferry ticket tucked behind a photograph: the ticket was scanned, the route was readable, and nobody yet knew which relative had kept it.", "output": "When Mara Ellis began the family photo catalogue, she expected to sort boxes by decade and write down the names she could still remember.
